baird-transatlantic-television-1928.summary: In 1928 Baird sent a television picture from London to New York by shortwave. Baird also gave colour television its first public demonstration and later built its first viable all-electronic colour picture tube.

dirac-equation-1928.summary: In 1928 Dirac's equation for the electron also predicted a particle of opposite charge. It described electron spin, until then added by hand, and accounted rigorously for hydrogen's fine spectral structure. It also admitted negative-energy solutions; rather than discard them, Dirac proposed that every particle has an oppositely charged partner, now called antimatter. Carl Anderson found that anti-electron, now called a positron, in 1933.

earhart-atlantic-1928.summary: In 1928 Amelia Earhart crossed the Atlantic by air as a passenger, first among women; in 1932 she flew it alone, solo and nonstop, another first for women, and received America's Distinguished Flying Cross. She promoted commercial air travel and wrote best-selling books, campaigning for women in aviation until she disappeared over Pacific waters on July 2, 1937, during her attempt to fly around the world.

eric-robot-1928.summary: In 1928 Eric, Britain's first robot, rose, bowed and gave a four-minute speech to open a London exhibition in place of a duke, with R.U.R. lettered on his chest after Karel Capek's 1920 play. Its guest, George VI (then Duke of York), had cancelled, and Richards offered to make a man of tin instead. Two people operated him, his voice arriving by radio; he could sit and stand but not walk. He toured America in 1929, then vanished; London's Science Museum rebuilt him in 2016.

gakutensoku-robot-1928.summary: In 1928 Makoto Nishimura displayed Gakutensoku, East Asia's first robot, in Kyoto; air pressure moved its hands and changed its expression. Its name means learning from nature's laws. Air pressure moved its head and hands and changed its facial expressions; it held a pen-shaped arrow in its right hand and an inspiration lamp in its left. After touring Japan, Korea and China in 1929 it vanished in the 1930s; Osaka Science Museum built its replica in 2008.

galvin-manufacturing-1928.summary: In 1928 Paul and Joseph Galvin founded the Chicago company that became Motorola, making devices to run battery radios on mains current. Paul coined Motorola for its car radio, joining motor with Victrola's -ola suffix, and adopted it as company name in 1947. Motorola later built two-way radios, walkie-talkies, pagers, cellular infrastructure and mobile phones, then split into two companies in 2011 after losing $4.3 billion from 2007 to 2009.

geiger-muller-tube-1928.summary: In 1928 Hans Geiger and Walther Muller improved Geiger's counter into a gas tube that clicked for every passing particle; radiation detection became cheap. Geiger had built a counter under Ernest Rutherford at Manchester in 1911, but it detected only alpha particles within bulky apparatus. Their gas-filled tube lets one ionising particle trigger a discharge cascade that registers as a click, and sensed alpha, beta and gamma radiation. Simple to build and cheap, Geiger counters became standard in physics, medicine and nuclear industry.

graf-zeppelin-1928.summary: In 1928 airship Graf Zeppelin began carrying passengers across the Atlantic, first to do so by air; it flew a million miles without a death. Built with public subscriptions and German government funds, and run by Luftschiffbau Zeppelin chairman Hugo Eckener, it was its era's longest and largest airship. Hydrogen gave it lift and Blau gas fuel extended its range, allowing airships' first circumnavigation and aviation's first nonstop Pacific crossing.

ibm-80-column-card-1928.summary: In 1928 IBM introduced the 80-column punched card; it defined the width of computer screens and code lines for 50 years. In 1927 Thomas J. Watson Sr. had asked inventors Clair D. Lake and J. Royden Pierce to fit more data onto cards without enlarging them; Pierce kept 45 round-hole columns storing more per column, while Lake's tightly spaced rectangular holes allowed 80 columns, nearly doubling capacity. By 1937 IBM's 32 presses in Endicott printed 5 to 10 million cards daily, and 80-column cards dominated data processing and fed early digital computers.

iron-lung-1928.summary: In 1928 Harvard engineers Drinker and Shaw built the iron lung, a tank that breathed for polio patients; it kept thousands alive until the vaccine. An electric motor drove pumps taken from two vacuum cleaners, changing air pressure inside an airtight metal box so that air moved in and out of a patient's lungs when their own muscles could not. Its first clinical use, at Boston Children's Hospital on October 12, 1928, revived an eight-year-old girl near death from polio within a minute. John Haven Emerson's cheaper version followed in 1931, and iron lungs became polio wards' defining machines.

penicillin-discovery-1928.summary: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed a mould killing bacteria on a dish, the observation behind antibiotics. Back at St Mary's Hospital, London, from his summer break, he found a Staphylococcus plate on which a blue-green Penicillium mould had grown and bacteria around it had not. He was examining plates with Daniel Merlin Pryce, his former student; one had been left with its lid open. Fleming showed this mould secreted an antibacterial substance, which he named penicillin on 7 March 1929. His own work ended that year; Howard Florey's Oxford team turned penicillin into a drug from 1939, and Fleming, Florey and Ernst Chain shared 1945's Nobel Prize.

pfleumer-magnetic-tape-1928.summary: In 1928 Fritz Pfleumer patented coating paper with iron oxide to record sound; magnetic tape stored music, data and video for 70 years. In 1927, after trying various materials, he glued iron oxide powder to very thin paper with lacquer, and received his patent in 1928. On 1 December 1932 he licensed AEG to use his invention in building Magnetophon K1, history's first practical tape recorder, demonstrated at Berlin's IFA fair in 1935.

prestressed-concrete-freyssinet-1928.summary: In 1928 Freyssinet patented prestressed concrete, with steel tendons stretched inside it. Concrete resists compression well but cracks under tension, so prestressing compresses it during production by tensioning high-strength steel tendons, single wires, strands or bars, within or alongside it. In service, loads that would pull ordinary concrete apart must first overcome this built-in squeeze. That lets engineers build longer spans with thinner members and less material than reinforced concrete allows, in bridges, high-rise floors, silos, pavements and nuclear containments.

queens-messenger-tv-drama-1928.summary: In September 1928 a General Electric station in Schenectady broadcast the first television drama to a handful of postcard-sized screens. Adapted from radio, it used several cameras picking up stage movement while microphones collected sound, with special-effect props to help actors' performances. Shown at 1:30 p.m. and again at 11:30 p.m., it was received at a station three miles away and on three-inch screens around Schenectady, and drew wide publicity.

raman-effect-1928.summary: In February 1928 C V Raman found light scattered by molecules changes colour slightly. Most light bounces off molecules unchanged, but a tiny fraction trades energy with molecular vibrations and shifts frequency, as Adolf Smekal had predicted in 1923. Grigory Landsberg and Leonid Mandelstam saw it independently in Moscow five days later. Raman received physics' 1930 Nobel Prize, and Raman spectroscopy, which reads those frequency shifts, became standard for identifying molecules.

royal-flying-doctor-service-1928.summary: In 1928 John Flynn started a flying doctor service in the Australian outback, to reach people far from any hospital. Pilot Clifford Peel had proposed using aircraft in 1917, and Flynn and Alfred Traeger developed pedal-powered radios so remote stations could call for help. Qantas supplied its first aircraft, a De Havilland DH.50, and Arthur Affleck piloted its first official flight 85 miles from Cloncurry to Julia Creek on 17 May 1928. It grew into Royal Flying Doctor Service.

sliced-bread-1928.summary: On 7 July 1928 Frank Bench's Chillicothe Baking Company in Missouri sold the first commercially sliced loaf, cut and wrapped by Otto Rohwedder's machine. In 1927 Rohwedder had finished a machine that both sliced loaves and wrapped them to keep slices fresh, and Bench bought his first. Continental Baking introduced sliced Wonder Bread in 1930, and by 1932 uniform slices had boosted sales of pop-up toasters.

southern-cross-trans-pacific-flight-1928.summary: Charles Kingsford Smith and Charles Ulm, with American navigator Harry Lyon and radio operator James Warner, left Oakland, California on 31 May 1928 in a Fokker F.VIIb-3m trimotor named Southern Cross. They flew to Honolulu, then 5,000 kilometres to Suva, Fiji, through storms with failing instruments, and on to Brisbane, landing at Eagle Farm on 9 June after 83 hours 38 minutes in air across 11,585 kilometres. Radio kept crew in touch with ships and shore. Crowds of thousands met them in Brisbane and Sydney. Flight opened prospects of air links between Australia and America, and Kingsford Smith and Ulm went on to cross Tasman Sea that September.

Disney had created Mickey Mouse after losing his character Oswald the Lucky Rabbit to Universal; two silent Mickey shorts already existed, but after seeing The Jazz Singer he held them back to make a fully synchronized sound cartoon. Its fully post-produced soundtrack set it apart from earlier sound cartoons, and it became Mickey's official debut; it entered America's public domain on January 1, 2024.

turkish-alphabet-reform-1928.summary: A language commission appointed in June 1928 adapts Latin letters to Turkish phonology in 29 letters, with ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş and ü, dropping q, w and x. Mustafa Kemal unveils it at a Gülhane Park gathering on 9 August, tours Anatolian towns with a blackboard, and on 1 November the Grand National Assembly passes Law 1353 making the new letters compulsory in public life from the new year and in all printing by June 1929. Nation Schools enrolled over a million adults in reading classes within two years. Arabic script had been used for Turkish for nine centuries but marked vowels poorly, and advocates argued Latin letters suited typewriters, telegraphs and mass schooling; critics noted the change cut a generation off from Ottoman texts. Soviet Turkic republics had switched to Latin letters in 1926 to 1928, before moving to Cyrillic in 1940.

byrd-south-pole-flight-1929.summary: In November 1929 Richard Byrd's crew flew over the South Pole and back in 19 hours, dropping an American flag there and dumping supplies to clear Antarctica's plateau. Bernt Balchen piloted, Harold June served as co-pilot and radioman, and Ashley McKinley photographed. Struggling for altitude over that plateau, they dumped empty fuel tanks and emergency supplies to clear it. Byrd claimed to be first to reach both poles by air, though his 1926 North Pole flight remains disputed on fuel-range grounds.

caton-thompson-great-zimbabwe-1929.summary: Gertrude Caton-Thompson, on a British Association commission, dug stratified trenches at Great Zimbabwe and nearby ruins in 1929 and reported that October that every detail in plan, building and contents seemed African Bantu, calling it inconceivable that a theory of Semitic origin could have arisen. Her finds of imported Chinese and Persian ceramics and glass beads in dated layers placed construction in medieval centuries, endorsing David Randall-MacIver's 1905 conclusion. Settler opinion in Southern Rhodesia rejected her, and successive colonial governments later pressured guides and museums to leave origins open, a dispute that ran until Zimbabwe's independence in 1980.

Hosted by AMPAS president Douglas Fairbanks, it recognised films released from August 1, 1927, to July 31, 1928, in 12 categories. Wings took Outstanding Picture, and Emil Jannings and Janet Gaynor won acting awards for multiple films.

frozen-food-birdseye-1929.summary: In 1929 Goldman Sachs and Postum paid $22 million for Clarence Birdseye's flash-freezing patents. Working as a field naturalist in Labrador between 1912 and 1915, Birdseye had watched Inuit freeze fresh fish almost instantly in Arctic air, and found that rapid freezing preserved texture and flavour better than slow freezing, which forms large ice crystals. He founded General Seafood in 1924 and built double-belt and multiplate freezers. In 1930 his new owners tested 26 frozen items in 18 Springfield, Massachusetts stores.

hubble-expanding-universe-1929.summary: In 1929 Hubble showed galaxies flee faster the farther away they are: the universe is expanding, so it once had a beginning. He combined his own distance measurements, since found badly off, built on Henrietta Swan Leavitt's methods, with redshifts chiefly measured by Vesto Slipher and Milton Humason. Alexander Friedmann had derived an expanding universe from general relativity in 1922, and Georges Lemaitre had predicted this proportionality in 1927, but Hubble's data gave cosmic expansion its first observational basis; his ratio became known as Hubble's constant.

Field studies ran 1929 to 1932 and were published in 1933. Researchers used questionnaires, interviews and content analysis. Reverend William H. Short of Motion Picture Research Council proposed them, and Ohio State's W. W. Charters directed researchers from several universities. They arose from post-war concern among educators and officials about movies' influence and efforts toward national motion-picture regulation, and are considered social science's first rigorous study of mass media.

traeger-pedal-radio-1929.summary: Adelaide engineer Alfred Traeger, working with Presbyterian minister John Flynn, built a transceiver powered by a bicycle-pedal generator producing about 20 watts at 300 volts, so that a station homestead without electricity could send Morse code over hundreds of kilometres. On 19 June 1929, Gertrude Rothery at Augustus Downs station sent first message to Cloncurry base of Flynn's Aerial Medical Service, later Royal Flying Doctor Service. Sets cost about 33 pounds. Traeger added a typewriter-style Morse keyboard in 1933 and voice transmission later, and his sets spread across Australia, Papua New Guinea and Africa. Pedal wireless underpinned School of the Air from 1951 and ended isolation for remote families.

wall-street-crash-1929.summary: In 1929 New York's stock market crashed; the Depression that followed put a quarter of Americans out of work. Small savers, disappointed by low bank interest, had poured money into stocks through brokers. On Black Thursday, October 24, a record 12.9 million shares traded; on Black Tuesday, October 29, some 16.4 million. Prices kept falling until July 8, 1932, erasing about 90% of pre-crash value, and confidence in banks eroded as it cascaded into a worldwide Great Depression; Congress answered with 1933's Glass-Steagall and Securities Acts.

chianan-irrigation-1930.summary: Completed in 1930 after ten years of construction under Japanese colonial engineer Hatta Yoichi, Wushantou reservoir and some 16,000 kilometres of canals and drains spread water across about 150,000 hectares of Chianan plain, where farmers had depended on erratic rain and salt-crusted soils. A semi-hydraulic fill dam, a 3-kilometre tunnel from Zengwen river and a three-year rotation of rice, sugarcane and dry crops governed allocation among villages. Rice and sugar output rose for export to Japan. Irrigation associations formed under this system still manage water, and Kuo's 2006 study estimates water needs for its paddy and upland rotation today.

cyclotron-1930.summary: In 1930 Ernest Lawrence described his cyclotron in Science, once his student had built a crude model: it whirls particles to high energy in a spiral. Earlier accelerators pushed particles through one electric field once; his design held charged particles on a spiral path with a magnet while a rapidly alternating field kicked them on each half-turn, so modest voltages produced high energies. Patented in 1932, cyclotrons produced neptunium and plutonium for Manhattan Project; Lawrence won physics' 1939 Nobel Prize.

east-texas-oil-field-1930.summary: In October 1930 a wildcatter's well was completed in the East Texas field, largest in America's lower 48 states; a resulting glut crashed prices and Texas rationed output. It was his third attempt, drilled by Ed Laster and named for Daisy Bradford, who owned its farm; wells spudded in 1927 and 1928 had been abandoned, and this one flowed oil on 5 September. Further strikes in December 1930 revealed a field covering 140,000 acres. Its wartime output justified Big Inch, a 1,400-mile pipeline to Philadelphia refineries.

freon-cfc-1930.summary: In 1930 Midgley's Freon made refrigerators safe, replacing toxic gases; forty years later it was found to be destroying the ozone layer. Refrigerators then ran on ammonia, chloromethane, propane or sulfur dioxide, all toxic, flammable or explosive; Freon was neither. Midgley had found in December 1921 that tetraethyl lead stopped engine knock, and in 1924 inhaled its vapour at a press conference to prove it safe. Leaded gasoline poisoned people, CFCs destroyed ozone, and 1987's Montreal Protocol phased Freon out.

Goddard had launched history's first liquid-fuelled rocket on March 16, 1926; Charles Lindbergh read of his work in The New York Times after a July 1929 launch and sought backers for him, hard to find after October's crash. With Guggenheim money Goddard moved to Roswell, New Mexico, and his team launched 34 rockets by 1941, reaching 2.6 km altitude and 885 km/h.

gulf-pearling-collapse-1930.summary: Pearl diving on oyster banks off Bahrain, Qatar and Trucial Coast towns had grown since the eighteenth century into these shaikhdoms' main livelihood; John Gordon Lorimer's 1905 survey counted 4,500 boats and 74,000 men, and export values rose eighteenfold between 1882 and 1912 as Paris and Bombay dealers bid for natural pearls. Mikimoto's round cultured pearls reached London and New York in quantity after 1919 at a fraction of natural prices, and in 1930 France's central bank stopped credit to pearl dealers, cutting values by most of their worth in a day. Bahrain's catch, valued at 1.5 million dollars in 1896, fell to 200,000 dollars by 1949. Divers and boat captains sank into debt, coastal towns emptied, and relief came only with oil royalties in Bahrain from 1932, Kuwait and Qatar after 1946 and Abu Dhabi in the 1960s.

keynes-economic-possibilities-1930.summary: In 1930 Keynes named technological unemployment, machines outrunning uses for labour, and foresaw 15-hour weeks. He meant unemployment caused by labour-saving discoveries outrunning society's ability to find new uses for labour, and called it "only a temporary phase of maladjustment". Within his readers' lifetimes, he thought, agriculture, mining and manufacturing might need a quarter of their accustomed human effort, and living standards in progressive countries would rise four to eight times within a century. He wrote: "Three-hour shifts or a fifteen-hour week may put off the problem for a great while."

neoprene-1930.summary: In spring 1930 DuPont chemist Arnold Collins made neoprene, the first commercially successful synthetic rubber in America; wetsuits and gaskets no longer needed a tree. Elmer K. Bolton had heard Notre Dame chemistry professor Julius Arthur Nieuwland lecture on how, while studying acetylene, he had made divinyl acetylene, a jelly that became rubber-like when passed over sulfur dichloride. DuPont bought Notre Dame's patent rights, and Wallace Carothers took over development, reacting monovinyl acetylene with hydrogen chloride to make chloroprene, which polymerises into neoprene. Announced as DuPrene in November 1931 and in production from 1932, it initially smelled foul until an improved process halved costs and removed odor.

Lowell Observatory telegraphed Harvard College Observatory on March 13, 1930. Hailed as ninth planet and named by 11-year-old Venetia Burney of Oxford, Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

Transparent tape extended that adhesive idea to sealing packages and repairing items, and during Great Depression households used it to mend rather than replace.

turksib-railway-completed-1930.summary: Turkestan-Siberian Railway, a tsarist scheme revived as a showcase of Stalin's first Five-Year Plan, runs 1,445 kilometres from Semipalatinsk on Siberia's trunk line south through Alma-Ata to Lugovaya on the Tashkent line. Construction crews of up to 50,000, many Kazakh herders newly recruited to wage labour, build south and north from 1927 across steppe, across the Ili river and over mountain passes, and join track at Aina-Bulak on 28 April 1930, eight months ahead of schedule. Matthew Payne's study shows how a building site became a school of Soviet industrial discipline, ethnic quotas and conflict. Turksib let Siberian grain and timber reach Central Asia so that irrigated land there could be turned to cotton, and it opened eastern Kazakhstan to settlement, mining and, during collectivisation, famine relief that came too late for many.

bulolo-gold-dredge-airlift-1931.summary: Alluvial gold at Edie Creek and Bulolo in New Guinea's Morobe district lay a week's walk from coast at Salamaua over 2,000-metre ranges with no road. Bulolo Gold Dredging, backed by Canadian Placer Development, ordered eight bucket dredges and had Guinea Airways carry every part by air in Junkers G 31 trimotors, each lifting about three tonnes. First dredge, flown in piece by piece, began working on 21 March 1932 after airlift started in 1931. By 1942 Guinea Airways had carried more freight than all other airlines combined, including power station, sawmill and whole township. Dredges produced gold worth more than 40 million pounds before Japanese invasion in 1942 halted operations.

differential-analyzer-1931.summary: In 1931 Vannevar Bush's differential analyser at MIT solved equations with spinning wheels and shafts. It solved differential equations by integration using six mechanical integrators, wheel-and-disc mechanisms that James Thomson had described in 1876, with epicyclic differentials for adding and subtracting. Bush first called it a "continuous integraph", then named it in a 1931 article. Douglas Hartree copied it at Manchester in 1934, and Moore School's machine computed artillery firing tables before ENIAC, which was modelled partly on it.

Because an electron's wavelength can be more than 100,000 times shorter than visible light's, such instruments resolve about 0.1 nanometre against roughly 200 for light microscopes. Ruska shared physics' 1986 Nobel Prize; Knoll had died in 1969.

empire-state-building-1931.summary: In 1931 the Empire State Building opened after 13 months of construction, 102 storeys and tallest building on earth until 1970. Its design changed fifteen times to guarantee it would be tallest of all buildings. Economic depression and World War II kept it unprofitable until the early 1950s. It stayed tallest until World Trade Center's North Tower topped out in 1970, and its Art Deco styling and observatories now draw about four million visitors yearly.

godel-incompleteness-1931.summary: In 1931 Gödel's first incompleteness theorem showed that any consistent system of axioms listable by an algorithm, and rich enough for arithmetic, contains true statements about natural numbers it cannot prove; his second shows such a system cannot prove its own consistency. They appeared as Theorem VI and Theorem XI of his paper "On Formally Undecidable Propositions in Principia Mathematica and Related Systems I." Together they ended Hilbert's program for a complete, consistent axiom set for all mathematics, and fed Church's and Turing's 1936 results on undecidability.

Congress had authorised it in 1928 after decades of studies on controlling floods, supplying irrigation water and generating hydroelectricity; Six Companies, Inc. won its contract and began work in early 1931 on an unprecedented structure, in torrid heat, with unproven techniques. Over 96 workers died. It impounds Lake Mead and powers Nevada, Arizona and California.

indian-statistical-institute-1931.summary: Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis registered Indian Statistical Institute on 17 December 1931 in Presidency College's statistical laboratory in Calcutta. He had been computing with hand calculators on anthropometric and flood data since 1920s and devised Mahalanobis distance in 1936. ISI pioneered large scale sample surveys, developed India's National Sample Survey from 1950, and published Sankhya from 1933. Under Mahalanobis it planned Second Five Year Plan's heavy industry model and installed India's first electronic computers, HEC-2M in 1956 and a Soviet URAL in 1958, training a generation of statisticians and computer scientists including C. R. Rao.

mechanical-tv-w2xab-1931.summary: In 1931 mechanical television, which scanned pictures with spinning discs, reached its peak. Early experimental systems all worked this way, but electronic scanning with cathode-ray tubes gave sharper images and superseded it in the mid-1930s. New York station W2XAB began mechanical broadcasts in 1931 and stopped on February 20, 1933, returning with an all-electronic system in 1939.

Berlin apothecary Eduard Simon had discovered it in 1839 after distilling an oily substance, styrene, from sweetgum resin and watching it thicken into jelly, later recognised as polymerisation. I. G. Farben succeeded once it built a reactor that extruded polystyrene through a heated tube and cutter into pellets. Clear, hard, brittle and cheap, polystyrene became one of our most widely used plastics, solid or foamed.

Standard Oil Company of California had founded BAPCO in Canada in 1929 and won Bahrain's only oil concession in 1930, operating under British rule and soon joined by Texaco. Shipments began in 1934, and in 1936 Bahrain opened the Gulf's first refinery outside Iran. Bahrain never produced great volumes, but this first American concession in the Middle East led its partners to Saudi Arabia's vast reserves and Aramco.

bbc-empire-service-1932.summary: In December 1932 BBC shortwave broadcasts to the Empire began, and King George V spoke to his subjects worldwide, in what became BBC World Service. In his first Christmas Message that year, George V said it served men and women so remote that only "voices out of the air" could reach them. Director-General John Reith warned listeners to expect little. Its first foreign-language service, Arabic, launched on 3 January 1938, and it grew into BBC World Service, broadcasting in more than 40 languages.

brave-new-world-1932.summary: In 1932 Huxley's Brave New World imagined a society kept content by engineered birth, drugs and pleasure, control without force. Set in a futuristic World State whose citizens are engineered before birth into an intelligence-based caste hierarchy, it anticipates advances in reproductive technology, sleep-learning and psychological manipulation. Huxley began it as a parody of H. G. Wells' utopian novels, and his reading of Henry Ford's My Life and Work shaped its mass-production society, dated After Ford. It critiques technological optimism common between the world wars and is often paired with Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four.

naharayim-hydroelectric-station-1932.summary: Pinhas Rutenberg, a Russian engineer and former revolutionary, won a concession from Britain's Mandate government in 1921, formalised in 1926 for seventy years, to use Jordan and Yarmuk waters for electricity. Emir Abdullah of Transjordan granted 6,000 dunams at Jisr al-Majami, and from 1927 some 3,000 workers built dams on both rivers, a canal and a storage lake feeding turbines through a 27-metre drop. A Yarmuk flood wrecked nearly finished works, delaying completion by a year. Abdullah pressed a starting switch on 9 June 1932 with High Commissioner Arthur Wauchope present. Three turbines gave 12 megawatts, raised to 18 in 1933, and high-tension lines carried power to Haifa, Tel Aviv and Amman's palace; Jerusalem stayed outside Rutenberg's concession. Iraqi forces took and wrecked this plant in May 1948 and it never ran again.

prontosil-sulfa-drug-1932.summary: In 1932 Domagk found that a red dye cured bacterial infections in mice; the first antibacterial drug saved his own daughter's arm. Chemists Josef Klarer and Fritz Mietzsch had synthesised it in a programme searching for dyes that might kill bacteria inside patients; until then medicine had disinfectants and antiseptic wound care but no drug for systemic infections. Results appeared on February 15, 1935 in Deutsche Medizinische Wochenschrift, Leonard Colebrook used it against puerperal fever, and this first sulfonamide drug opened antimicrobial chemotherapy; Domagk received medicine's 1939 Nobel Prize.

sharjah-air-station-1932.summary: Imperial Airways had flown its India route along Iran's Gulf coast since 1929 under a three-year arrangement Tehran refused to renew. Britain's political residency pressed Trucial rulers for an alternative, and on 22 July 1932 Shaikh Sultan bin Saqr al-Qasimi of Sharjah signed an agreement for an air station: 800 rupees a month in landing fees, a personal subsidy of 500 rupees, a promise that British ships would call at Sharjah, and his undertaking to build a walled rest house guarded by his own men. At 4 pm on 5 October 1932 Handley Page HP42 Hanno arrived from Gwadar with four passengers. Weekly, then twice-weekly, airliners refuelled and passengers slept at Al Mahatta fort; Royal Air Force squadrons used this field through World War II. Sharjah's airfield preceded oil concessions and put Trucial Coast towns on imperial maps.

sukkur-barrage-1932.summary: Viceroy Willingdon opened Lloyd Barrage at Sukkur on 13 January 1932 after nine years of construction under Arnold Musto's design. Sixty six gates each 60 feet wide span Indus below Rohri gorge; seven canals, four on left bank and three on right, carry water through over 6,000 miles of channels. Gross command area was about 7.5 million acres, converting Sind's flood-dependent inundation farming to controlled perennial irrigation of wheat, cotton and rice. It remained largest single irrigation work in world for decades and still feeds a quarter of Pakistan's canal-irrigated land. Waterlogging, salinity and silting have required continuous remodelling.

Under John Bradfield of New South Wales Public Works, British firm Dorman Long of Middlesbrough built it from 1923, patterning it on New York's Hell Gate Bridge; sixteen workers died. At its opening a New Guard member on horseback slashed its ribbon with his sword before Premier Jack Lang could cut it. Nicknamed "the Coathanger", it carries rail, vehicle, bicycle and pedestrian traffic and is still tallest among steel arch bridges at 134 m.

Disney agreed, scrapping black-and-white footage already shot. It won the first Academy Award for Best Cartoon Short Subject, and Disney's exclusive Technicolor contract, running to end of 1935, left rivals with inferior two-colour processes.

technocracy-movement-1932.summary: In August 1932 Howard Scott's Technocrats claimed machines were causing the Depression's unemployment and proposed rule by engineers. Technological improvements had come so rapidly in three years, he said, that only 55 per cent of workers thrown out of work by the downturn could be re-employed even if industry resumed its 1929 peak production. Scott was directing head of Technocracy, described as a research body seeking an engineering approach to economic problems. His argument fed a wider 1930s debate over technological unemployment.

boeing-247-1933.summary: In 1933 the Boeing 247 flew coast to coast in under 20 hours, eight hours faster than Ford Trimotors or Curtiss Condors. It was among the first airliners with all-metal semimonocoque construction, a fully cantilevered wing and retractable landing gear, plus trim tabs, an autopilot and de-icing boots. Boeing sold its first 60 to its affiliated airline for $65,000 each, and refused TWA, which turned to Douglas; carrying only 10 passengers, Boeing's design was soon eclipsed by Douglas's roomier DC-2 and DC-3.

century-of-progress-1933.summary: In 1933 Chicago's Century of Progress fair showed streamlined trains and houses of tomorrow to a Depression crowd under its unofficial motto "Science Finds, Industry Applies, Man Conforms." Planned before 1929's crash and financed by selling memberships rather than public money, it argued that science, technology and industry would bring recovery. Its multicoloured Moderne buildings, Sky Ride transporter bridge and Homes of Tomorrow exhibition drew such crowds that it reopened from 26 May to 31 October 1934.

fireside-chats-1933.summary: In March 1933 Roosevelt explained the banking crisis by radio to tens of millions of homes; a leader could now speak to a nation at once. He had spent that week fighting a month-long epidemic of bank closures, shutting America's entire banking system on March 6. Speaking with familiarity to millions over radio, he quelled rumours, bypassed hostile newspapers and explained policies directly. CBS executive Harry C. Butcher coined "fireside chat" before his May 7, 1933 address, and his evening talks continued through 1944.

fm-radio-armstrong-1933.summary: In December 1933 Armstrong patented FM radio, which carried music without static; the networks and RCA fought it for 20 years. Static from thunderstorms and electrical equipment plagued amplitude-modulation radio, and Armstrong, working secretly in a basement laboratory at Columbia University, found that swinging a carrier's frequency far wider than its audio signal rejected noise far better. He showed it to RCA president David Sarnoff in 1934 and tested it from Empire State Building until October 1935, but RCA declined to back it; decades of litigation followed, ending with his suicide in 1954.

jansky-radio-astronomy-1933.summary: In 1933 Karl Jansky of Bell Labs found radio waves coming from the centre of the Milky Way. Assigned to trace static troubling transatlantic shortwave telephony, he had built a 100-foot rotating antenna at Holmdel, New Jersey, tuned to 20.5 MHz, and found a faint hiss peaking every 23 hours and 56 minutes, one sidereal day, which astrophysicist Albert Skellett told him pointed to stars, not Sun. Neither astronomers nor Depression-era Bell Labs pursued it; Grote Reber's 1937 backyard telescope began radio astronomy proper.

london-tube-map-beck-1933.summary: In 1933 Harry Beck drew the London Underground as a circuit diagram, ignoring geography. Beck, an Underground employee, had drawn it in 1931, reasoning that since trains ran mostly underground, riders needed only route topology: stations joined by straight segments running vertically, horizontally or at 45 degrees, with ticks for ordinary stations, diamonds for interchanges and only River Thames as landmark. Paid ten guineas for his card edition, Beck kept designing Tube maps until 1960, and his approach spread to transit maps worldwide.

plexiglas-pmma-1933.summary: In 1933 Röhm trademarked acrylic sheet as Plexiglas, with Rohm and Haas sheet production from 1936; a clear plastic replaced glass in cockpits and later in aquariums and signs. He trademarked it after casting work in Darmstadt in 1932 and 1933; chemists in several laboratories, including Röhm and Walter Bauer, had developed poly(methyl methacrylate) in 1928, and Britain's ICI had its own version, Perspex, on sale in 1933. Known generically as acrylic, this transparent thermoplastic serves as a lightweight, shatter-resistant alternative to glass.

polyethylene-ici-1933.summary: In 1933 two ICI chemists made polyethylene by accident under high pressure; it became the most produced plastic on Earth. Applying several hundred atmospheres of pressure to ethylene mixed with benzaldehyde, they produced a white, waxy material; Hans von Pechmann had made it by accident in 1898, but from unstable diazomethane. Trace oxygen contamination had started their reaction, so it resisted repetition until ICI chemist Michael Perrin devised a reproducible high-pressure process in 1935. Industrial production began in 1939, and polyethylene is now Earth's most produced plastic.

Other nations soon built their own services; telex spread across Europe, then worldwide after 1945, and became business's main medium for electronic text messages until fax machines displaced it in the 1980s.

tennessee-valley-authority-1933.summary: In May 1933 Congress created the Tennessee Valley Authority for navigation, flood control, electricity, fertiliser manufacturing and regional planning in Tennessee Valley, a region that suffered worse Depression-era poverty and poorer infrastructure than most. Senator George Norris had fought since 1920 to keep Muscle Shoals' hydroelectric site public. TVA broke ground on Norris Dam on October 1, 1933, built 29 hydroelectric dams, and remains America's largest public utility.

uk-national-grid-1933.summary: In September 1933 Britain completed its National Grid's regional networks, run separately with emergency interconnections until a 1937 trial and as one national system from 1938, letting electricity generated anywhere meet demand elsewhere. In 1925 ministers had asked industrialist Lord Weir to fix Britain's fragmented supply industry, and his Electricity (Supply) Act 1926 created Central Electricity Board to build a synchronised nationwide AC grid at 132 kV and 50 Hz. Some 6,400 kilometres of mostly overhead cables linked its 122 most efficient power stations, from a first tower erected near Edinburgh on 14 July 1928.

chrysler-airflow-1934.summary: In 1934 Chrysler's Airflow was the first American car designed in a wind tunnel; buyers hated its looks, and streamlining waited a decade. Engineer Carl Breer's team had tested at least 50 scale models in a wind tunnel, with Orville Wright's cooperation, and adopted unibody construction for rigidity with less weight. Its merged hood, waterfall grille and headlamps looked alien; production peaked at 6,212 in May 1934, General Motors ran advertising discrediting it, and Chrysler's conventional models far outsold it. Production ended in 1937; rivals gradually adopted its aerodynamic ideas.

communications-act-1934.summary: In June 1934 Congress created the Federal Communications Commission to regulate radio and telephones under a public-interest standard. It replaced Federal Radio Commission and took over interstate telephone regulation from Interstate Commerce Commission regulators, putting wire and radio communication under one regulator, a first. Codified as Title 47, United States Code, it governed American telecommunications until 1996's Telecommunications Act, its first major overhaul in nearly 62 years.

Hays, had adopted its Production Code of self-censorship in 1930 but enforced it loosely; a June 13, 1934 amendment created PCA and made its seal compulsory. Its code listed unacceptable content, from drugs to sexual matters, and Breen administered it until 1954. Enforcement held well into the 1950s, weakened under television and foreign films, and ended in 1968 with MPAA's ratings system.

mumford-technics-and-civilization-1934.summary: In 1934 Lewis Mumford's Technics and Civilization argued clocks, rather than steam engines, were the modern age's key machine. He traced modern technology's roots to medieval times rather than the Industrial Revolution, and divided its development into three overlapping phases: eotechnic, from Greek for dawn, paleotechnic and neotechnic. His eotechnic phase, AD 1000 to 1800, begins with clocks, which he called a prototype for all other machines and capitalism's most important basis, since they made time fungible.

muzak-1934.summary: In 1934 George Squier named his wired background-music service Muzak, music crossed with Kodak. Squier, credited with inventing telephone carrier multiplexing in 1910, had patented ways of sending signals over electrical lines; in 1922 utility conglomerate North American Company bought his patent rights and formed Wired Radio, Inc., delivering music to customers and charging on their electric bills. By 1934 free, advertising-supported radio had eclipsed wired music at home, so Squier refocused on commercial clients, shops and offices. Muzak became shorthand for background music everywhere.

Budd Company built its three articulated stainless-steel cars for Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad, joining them by shotwelding and using unibody construction to save weight. Retired in 1960, it stands in Chicago's Museum of Science & Industry.

weizmann-institute-1934.summary: In 1934 Chaim Weizmann founded a research institute in Rehovot fourteen years before Israel existed. He invited Nobel laureate Fritz Haber to direct it, but Haber died on his way to Palestine, so Weizmann took charge himself and pursued organic chemistry in its laboratories until becoming Israel's president in February 1949. On 2 November 1949, with Sieff family's agreement, it was renamed Weizmann Institute of Science. It built WEIZAC, among history's first electronic computers, in 1954 and 1955, and now employs about 3,800 scientists, students and staff.

cane-toads-queensland-1935.summary: In June 1935 entomologist Reginald Mungomery brought 102 cane toads (Rhinella marina) from Hawai'i to Meringa near Cairns, bred them, and in August released about 2,400 young toads into sugar cane fields around Gordonvale to control greyback and Frenchi cane beetles. Toads could not reach beetles high on cane stalks and ignored them, but bred prolifically in Queensland's wet tropics. Within decades they spread south to New South Wales and west across Northern Territory, reaching Western Australia by 2009 at rates up to 50 kilometres a year. Toxic skin glands kill quolls, goannas and snakes that eat them. Shine's 2010 review found severe but patchy ecological impacts.

Weekly passenger flights began in October 1936, San Francisco to Manila with overnight stops at Honolulu, Midway, Wake and Guam. All three were lost in service, Hawaii Clipper vanishing in 1938.

Plants stand 60 to 110 centimeters instead of 150, so they carry heavy fertilizer and grain without lodging. USDA adviser S. Cecil Salmon collects seed in occupied Japan in 1946; Orville Vogel at Washington State crosses it with Brevor, and in late 1952 Norman Borlaug learns of Vogel's results and obtains seed for Mexico. Dwarfing genes Rht1 and Rht2 from Norin 10 underpin Borlaug's Pitic 62 and Penjamo 62 and most of the world's wheat today.

kodachrome-1935.summary: In April 1935 Kodak announced Kodachrome, a three-colour film developed by Leopold Godowsky Jr. and Leopold Mannes, professional musicians and university-trained scientists. Earlier colour films such as Autochrome and Dufaycolor used additive screens of discrete colour elements that showed on enlargement; Kodachrome stacked emulsion layers in one film and added dyes during processing, becoming history's first mass-marketed subtractive colour film. Its complex processing meant customers mailed film to Kodak; manufacture lasted 74 years, ending in 2009.

magnetophon-tape-1935.summary: In 1935 AEG showed the Magnetophon, the first practical tape recorder; after the war Allied engineers carried it home and radio changed. Its engineers had built this reel-to-reel machine on Fritz Pfleumer's magnetic tape invention, with tape manufactured by BASF. Later models added AC tape bias, which largely eliminated background hiss; reproduction improved so far that industry insiders could not tell recordings from live play, and Hitler used such machines to deliver apparently live broadcasts from cities he had left. In 1945 US Army officer Jack Mullin brought captured Magnetophons home, seeding Ampex and American tape recording.

nylon-1935.summary: In 1935 Carothers at DuPont made nylon, the first fully synthetic fibre; stockings, parachutes and ropes no longer needed silk. DuPont had begun its polymer research programme in 1927, letting small teams pursue pioneering chemistry; his team had already produced neoprene. Nylon's first commercial use came in toothbrush bristles in 1938, and women's stockings, shown at 1939 New York World's Fair and sold nationwide from 1940, sold 64 million pairs in their first year, cutting silk imports from Japan. Paul Schlack at IG Farben answered with nylon 6 in 1938.

parking-meter-1935.summary: On 16 July 1935 the first parking meter went up in Oklahoma City; kerb space became something a city could charge for. Engineering professors Holger George Thuesen and Gerald A. Hale of Oklahoma State University had begun work in 1933 at lawyer and newspaper publisher Carl C. Magee's request, and their first working meter, Black Maria, appeared in 1935. Roger W. Babson had patented a meter in 1928, but it needed power from each parked car's battery. Magee's spring-driven meters needed periodic winding by service workers. Drivers challenged them in court in 1936 and 1937, and judges ruled that free use of streets was no absolute right.

penguin-paperbacks-1935.summary: In 1935 Allen Lane launched Penguin paperbacks at sixpence, as much as a packet of cigarettes, sold through Woolworths and other shops. Lane said poor reading matter on sale at Exeter St Davids railway station had inspired him to publish cheap, well-designed quality books. They carried fiction and non-fiction in plain covers of three horizontal bands, colour-coded by series, and brought quality literature to a mass audience.

prontosil-sulfonamide-1935.summary: In 1935 Prontosil, a red dye, became the first drug to cure bacterial infections, a decade before penicillin. It was sulfonamides' first member and among medicine's earliest antimicrobials; Leonard Colebrook introduced it as treatment for puerperal fever in maternity wards, and Alexander Ashley Weech treated America’s first patient with it in 1935. Late that year, Ernest Fourneau’s Pasteur Institute laboratory showed that Prontosil breaks down in the body to sulfanilamide, a simpler colorless molecule Bayer had patented in 1909 without seeing its use.

puhca-1935.summary: In 1935 the United States broke up the utility holding companies whose collapse had ruined investors. In June 1932 Middle West Utilities, a holding company operating in 39 states, had gone bankrupt and destroyed hundreds of thousands of small investors' savings, and a seven-year Federal Trade Commission investigation had exposed how pyramided holding companies escaped state regulation. PUHCA gave Securities and Exchange Commission power to regulate, license and break up electric utility holding companies, limiting each to one integrated system within one state. Energy Policy Act of 2005 repealed it.

reichsautobahn-1935.summary: In 1935 Germany opened its first Reichsautobahn, propaganda for Hitler and a model for motorways worldwide. Weimar-era groups had planned long-distance motorways, and two short controlled-access roads existed, but Hitler's party, after opposing such plans, embraced them on taking power and presented them as Hitler's own idea. Todt's report made its case; Hitler turned its first sod at Frankfurt on 23 September 1933, where 720 unemployed men were invested with shovels. Its first 1,000 km were complete by September 1936.

studio-misr-cairo-1935.summary: Talaat Harb, founder of Banque Misr in 1920, created the Misr Company for Acting and Cinema in 1925 to make documentaries and by 1935 had decided feature films came next. Studio Misr was inaugurated in Giza on 12 October 1935 with sound stages, laboratories and editing rooms bought from Europe, staffed by Egyptians he had sent to train in Germany, among them Ahmed Badrakhan and cinematographer Hassan Mourad, alongside German director Fritz Kramp. Its first feature, Wedad with Umm Kulthum, appeared in 1936. Viola Shafik's history of Arab cinema treats this studio as where Egyptian film became an industry that supplied Arabic-speaking audiences from Morocco to Iraq.

wirephoto-1935.summary: In 1935 the Associated Press began sending news photographs over telephone lines; a picture could reach front pages the same day. Its first wired photo showed a small plane's December 1934 crash in New York's Adirondacks. When US Navy airship USS Macon crashed into the Pacific on 12 February 1935, Wirephoto transmitted its first drawing, staff artist Noel Sickles' conceptual sketch of crash and rescue, after staff hesitated because it was not a photo; a photograph of survivors coming ashore followed overnight for next morning's papers. AP held its trademark on "AP Wirephoto" from 1963 to 2004.

bbc-television-service-1936.summary: In November 1936 the BBC began the first regular high-definition television service from Alexandra Palace, to a few hundred sets in London. The BBC had broadcast 30-line mechanical pictures from Broadcasting House since 1932; now Baird's system and Marconi-EMI's all-electronic 405-line system alternated for a six-month trial. Baird's mechanical film cameras proved cumbersome and visually inferior, and his system closed in February 1937. By September 1939 British makers had built 18,999 sets, when war shut transmissions for fear they would guide enemy aircraft.

douglas-dc-3-1936.summary: In 1936 Douglas's DC-3 entered service, among the first airliners able to profit from passengers alone, without mail subsidies. Cruising at 207 mph with 21 to 32 passengers and 1,500 miles of range, it crossed America eastbound in about 15 hours with three stops. By 1939 about 90% of airline flights worldwide used DC-3s or variants; with military C-47s, production passed 16,000.

hoover-dam-1936.summary: In March 1936 Hoover Dam was handed to federal officials two years early; it tamed the Colorado and powered the Southwest's growth. Six Companies, Inc. had built it since 1931, through torrid heat, with over 96 workers dying, and President Roosevelt had dedicated it on September 30, 1935. In late 1936 Lake Mead rose high enough for its first three generators to start, and its power now serves Nevada, Arizona and California.

lambda-calculus-1936.summary: In 1936 Alonzo Church published his lambda calculus, which expresses computation through defining and applying functions, with variable binding and substitution. His original system of the early 1930s had proved inconsistent in 1935, when Stephen Kleene and J. B. Rosser found a paradox. His 1936 paper also proved that no algorithm can decide whether two lambda expressions are equivalent, history's first undecidability proof. Lambda calculus can simulate any Turing machine and vice versa, and functional programming languages implement it.

life-magazine-photojournalism-1936.summary: In November 1936 Henry Luce launched Life as a weekly of photographs; Americans saw the news before they read it. Convinced that pictures could tell stories rather than merely illustrate text, he condensed words into captions for 50 pages of photographs, printed on heavily coated paper and sold for a dime. Margaret Bourke-White's photograph of Fort Peck Dam in Montana filled its first cover. Circulation leapt from 380,000 copies of that issue to more than a million a week within four months, and Life became photojournalism's defining American magazine.

modern-times-1936.summary: In 1936 Chaplin's Modern Times showed his Tramp on a Depression-era assembly line, where pace and repetition bring on a nervous breakdown and leave him stuck inside factory machinery. Chaplin drew on conditions he saw touring Europe and on his conversation with Mahatma Gandhi about modern technology. It was his Tramp's last appearance, and among the first 25 films chosen for America's National Film Registry.

rural-electrification-act-1936.summary: In May 1936 the United States began lending to farmer cooperatives to string power lines; a tenth of farms had power, by 1953 nine in ten. Electricity was then commonplace in cities but largely unavailable on farms and ranches. Loans went through member-owned cooperatives that bought power wholesale and strung their own lines, hundreds of which still exist. Rayburn said in 1959 that 90 percent of farm homes had electricity, against three percent in the early 1930s.

turing-computable-numbers-1936.summary: In 1936 Alan Turing described an imaginary machine that could run any computation: the blueprint for computers. It describes an abstract machine that reads and writes symbols on an unbounded tape according to a table of rules, simple enough to analyse yet able to run any algorithm, and a universal machine that computes any computable sequence given another machine's encoded instructions. With it Turing proved that Hilbert's decision problem, whether every mathematical statement can be mechanically proved or disproved, has no solution. Alonzo Church, his doctoral advisor, named it "Turing machine"; their work underpins computer science.

chain-home-radar-1937.summary: By 1937 Britain's Chain Home radar stations watched the approaches to London; in 1940 they let a few fighters meet every raid. In late 1934 Tizard Committee had asked Robert Watson-Watt about rumoured German radio death rays; his assistant Arnold Wilkins showed such rays impossible but proposed detecting aircraft by radio echoes, demonstrated in February 1935. Chain Home transmitters flooded airspace with shortwave pulses and receivers measured echoes' direction and range, roughly 100 miles, with height-finding added in early 1937. Linked through Dowding system to fighter controllers, it let RAF watch Luftwaffe formations assembling over France in 1940.

elixir-sulfanilamide-1937.summary: In 1937 a sulfa medicine dissolved in antifreeze killed over 100 people, many children; the United States required drugs to be proven safe. Its chief chemist, Harold Watkins, had dissolved sulfanilamide in diethylene glycol with raspberry flavouring, unaware that DEG causes kidney failure; no law required premarket safety testing, and Massengill did none. By October 11 American Medical Association had reports of deaths, and FDA inspectors hunted down distributed bottles. At least 100 people died. Massengill's owner denied responsibility, Watkins killed himself awaiting trial, and public outrage drove 1938's Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

hindenburg-disaster-1937.summary: In May 1937 the airship Hindenburg burned in 34 seconds at Lakehurst, filmed and broadcast. Filled with flammable hydrogen, it had made ten uneventful trips to America after its maiden flight in March 1936. Of 97 people aboard, 13 passengers and 22 crewmen died, plus one ground crewman. Newsreel cameras, photographers and Herbert Morrison's recorded radio report, broadcast next day, carried its destruction worldwide; ignition's cause remains debated. Public confidence in giant rigid airships collapsed, ending their era.

houdry-catalytic-cracking-1937.summary: In 1937 the first catalytic cracking plant opened in Pennsylvania, turning heavy oil into high-octane petrol for cars and warplanes. Eugene Houdry, a French engineer, had sought from 1922 to make gasoline from lignite with catalysts, and solved what had stymied others: catalysts quickly coated with coke and stopped working, so he devised a method to regenerate them. After French government support ended in 1930 he moved to America and worked with Socony Vacuum and Sun Oil on pilot plants. By 1942, 14 Houdry fixed-bed units were producing high-octane aviation fuel for Allied armed forces.

PCM measures an analogue signal's amplitude at regular intervals and records each sample as a binary number, so a wave becomes a stream of digits that noise cannot corrupt as it degrades analogue signals. Reeves described its theory and advantages and filed his French patent in 1938, but no practical application followed. SIGSALY, which carried high-level Allied communications in World War II, made digital speech's first transmission, and PCM later became digital audio's and telephony's standard.

It showed Boolean algebra, nineteenth-century logic of true and false, could describe arrangements of electrical switches and relays, so circuits could be analysed with equations, simplified by algebra and made to perform logical and arithmetic functions. Using switches' binary properties this way became digital circuit design's foundation.

Its 200,000-copy print run sold out, and once National Allied Publications realised Superman drove sales, circulation approached a million a month, launching superhero comics. Production peaked at 2.4 million barrels per day in 1972, stood near 1.7 million in 2005, and in 2010 still supplied half of Kuwait's oil.

Trucks carried fuel and munitions from Rangoon over 24 switchbacks of Twenty-Four Zig Road and across Salween and Mekong gorges. Japan's occupation of Burma in 1942 cut route until Ledo Road reconnected it in 1945. Chinese and American accounts differ on how much tonnage reached Chongqing, but road sustained Nationalist resistance for three years.

It cuts, threshes and cleans grain with its own engine, needing no tractor and opening a field without a trampled first round, but it is too heavy and costly for volume production. In early 1944 sales manager Joe Tucker persuades the US War Production Board to release steel for 500 extra No. 21s by promising to cut one million acres; sold only to custom operators moving north from Texas, this Harvest Brigade cuts 1,019,500 acres and over 25 million bushels, and founds custom combining as a trade.

On June 7, 1938, Cárdenas created Petróleos Mexicanos with exclusive rights over oil, and companies and foreign governments boycotted Mexican oil. After those sanctions Mexico paid compensation near asset value, settled as World War II's alliance formed, and March 18 is now a Mexican civic holiday.

They had found barium, an element about half uranium's mass, among their products. Lise Meitner, who had fled Berlin for Sweden in July 1938, and her nephew Otto Robert Frisch explained it theoretically in January 1939, and Frisch named it fission after cell division. One uranium-235 atom's fission releases about 100 million times more energy than burning one carbon atom. Because fission emits further neutrons, it can sustain a chain reaction, which led to nuclear reactors and atomic bombs.

Fiberglass traps many small air cells with a bonding agent, giving light, low-density insulation. Owens-Corning introduced continuous filament glass fibres, which reinforce plastics in boats, pipes and other composites, and Fiberglas became a genericised trademark; Owens-Corning remains glass fibre's major producer.

trans-iranian-railway-completed-1938.summary: Iran's Majles voted a state monopoly on tea and sugar in 1925 and a railway law in February 1927 so that a north-south line could be built without foreign loans, a condition shaped by memories of Qajar concessions. An American-German syndicate began at both ends in 1927; after payment disputes Danish firm Kampsax took over supervision in 1933 and split construction into 43 lots for contractors from a dozen countries and Iran. Reza Shah tightened a final bolt in Lorestan on 26 August 1938, eleven years after breaking ground, linking Bandar Shah on the Caspian with Bandar Shahpur on the Gulf via Tehran. Allied forces used this line to carry supplies to the Soviet Union after occupying Iran in 1941.

zuse-z1-1938.summary: In 1938 Konrad Zuse finished the Z1 in his parents' living room in Berlin, a mechanical computer that read programs from punched film. It was a binary, electrically driven mechanical computer, financed completely by private funds, reading instructions from perforated 35 mm film and working on 22-bit floating-point numbers with a 16-word memory. Some 20,000 thin metal sheets, cut with a jigsaw, formed its logic; it was freely programmable but unreliable in operation. Allied bombing destroyed it in December 1943.

dakar-yellow-fever-vaccine-1939.summary: At Institut Pasteur de Dakar, Jean Laigret, Max Peltier and Constant Durieux developed a yellow fever vaccine from a virus strain isolated in Senegal in 1927 and attenuated by passage through mouse brains. Their freeze-dried single dose could be scratched into skin together with smallpox vaccine, letting a team immunise up to 800 people an hour. Mass campaigns across French West Africa began in 1939; about 14 million people were vaccinated in wartime and 56 million by 1953, and urban yellow fever epidemics there stopped. Cases of encephalitis, mostly in children, were recorded but poorly reported, as Aro Velmet shows, and use in children was restricted in 1961 and ended in the 1980s.

ddt-insecticide-1939.summary: In 1939 Paul Muller found DDT killed insects; it stopped typhus and malaria for millions and then poisoned birdlife. Armies used it in World War II's second half to limit malaria and typhus, and it went on public sale in the United States by October 1945. He received 1948's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this discovery. Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring focused opposition to its environmental harm in 1962, and its agricultural use has been banned worldwide under the Stockholm Convention since 2004.

Szilard visited Einstein at Cutchogue, Long Island, on July 12, 1939; Einstein, who had not considered fission as a weapon, said "Daran habe ich gar nicht gedacht" and agreed to sign, doing so on August 2. Germany's invasion of Poland delayed Alexander Sachs's meeting with Roosevelt until October 11, 1939, after which Roosevelt authorized the Advisory Committee on Uranium under Lyman Briggs.

elektro-robot-1939.summary: In 1939 Westinghouse showed Elektro at the New York World's Fair, a seven-foot robot that walked on voice command and spoke 700 words. J.M. Barnett, Jack Weeks Sr., Harold Gorsuch, and other engineers built it at Westinghouse Electric Corporation's Mansfield, Ohio, facility. Seven feet tall and 265 pounds, it walked by voice command, spoke about 700 words from a 78-rpm record player, smoked cigarettes and blew up balloons; its steel gear, cam and motor skeleton wore an aluminum skin, and photoelectric eyes told red light from green. A robot dog, Sparko, joined it in 1940. Restored, Elektro is displayed at Mansfield Memorial Museum.

It grew from his 1937 Shell Oil City of Tomorrow model and presented his vision of 1959 to 1960, 20 years ahead, with automated highways and vast suburbs. Futurama first put a nationwide expressway network before mass audiences, and GM built a working automated-highway prototype by 1960.

heinkel-he-178-jet-1939.summary: In August 1939 Heinkel's He 178 made the first flight on turbojet power, days before the Second World War began. It flew on Hans von Ohain’s engine, which Heinkel developed in secrecy, concealed even from Luftwaffe leaders. That flight lasted six minutes and almost ended in disaster during its unpowered landing approach. With 598 km/h top speed and short endurance, it failed to impress Nazi officials at a demonstration on 1 November 1939, and German jet development passed to other programmes.

hydramatic-transmission-1939.summary: In October 1939 General Motors announced the first mass-produced automatic gearbox, shipping 1940-model Oldsmobile Series 60 and 70 cars with it at $57 for the option; driving no longer needed a clutch. Cadillac engineers under Earl Thompson had worked on "shiftless" transmissions since 1932; Hydra-Matic paired hydraulically shifted planetary gears with a fluid coupling in place of a friction clutch, so drivers never declutched, and offered four forward speeds plus reverse. Almost 200,000 had sold when passenger car production stopped for war work in February 1942.

new-york-worlds-fair-1939.summary: In 1939 New York's World's Fair sold its World of Tomorrow to slightly over 45 million visitors across two seasons; television was demonstrated publicly there. President Roosevelt opened it on April 30, 1939, with 62 nations and more than 1,400 organizations and companies exhibiting around Trylon and Perisphere, its theme center. RCA and NBC ran television demonstrations, among them the first televised Major League Baseball game; Westinghouse showed Elektro, General Motors ran Futurama, and nylon made its debut. War in Europe four months later closed or shrank several exhibits.

He had convinced United Aircraft's directors in 1938 that his years of rotary-wing research would pay off; this first experimental machine used a single three-blade main rotor driven by a 75 horsepower engine. Its first free flight took place on 13 May 1940, making it America's first successful single lifting rotor helicopter.

Its operator chose with a wrist bar between a buzz tone for vowels and nasals, pitch set by foot pedal, and hiss for sibilants, then shaped each sound through filters with fifteen keys; the console demanded highly trained operators.

Plasma, blood's cell-free fluid, treats shock and keeps without refrigeration, so it suited combat; dried plasma shipped as two tin cans, one holding distilled water, and was ready about three minutes after mixing. Planned as a rehearsal for national blood banking, it led to the American Red Cross National Blood Donor Service in November 1941.

cavity-magnetron-1940.summary: In 1940 Randall and Boot built a cavity magnetron; in mass production by early 1941, it made radar small enough for aircraft, and it now heats food in microwave ovens. Wartime radar needed high power at about 10 cm wavelength, far shorter than existing tubes could manage at 50 to 150 cm. Their tube swept electrons past small open cavities cut in a metal block, under a magnetic field, and made them ring at microwave frequencies. It produced about 400 watts, unprecedented output at 10 cm. After 1945 this same device came to power microwave ovens.

gonzalez-camarena-color-tv-1940.summary: On 19 August 1940 Guillermo González Camarena, a 23-year-old engineer at Mexico City radio station XEFO, filed a Mexican patent for a 'sistema tricromático secuencial de campos', a colour television method using a rotating disc of red, green and blue filters synchronised at camera and receiver. The US Patent Office granted him patent 2,296,019 in 1942. He built cameras and receivers in his own workshop from salvaged parts, demonstrated colour pictures to Mexican officials, and in 1946 opened experimental station XE1GC. Camarena's station XHGC, channel 5, broadcast from 1952; Mexico's first colour transmissions followed in 1963. Andrés Burbano's study places his work alongside parallel field-sequential systems by Baird and CBS's Peter Goldmark.

Treated as a yardstick for limited-access roads, it became a model for later toll roads.

tacoma-narrows-bridge-collapse-1940.summary: In November 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted apart in a 40 mile an hour wind on film; bridges have been tested in wind tunnels since. Leon Moisseiff’s design used shallow, narrow plate girders that left its deck too flexible. Textbooks often call this failure resonance, but moderate wind set off aeroelastic flutter, a self-exciting twist that grew without bound above about 35 mph. It collapsed into the strait, and its central span fell into the water, five days after Frederick Farquharson’s wind-tunnel study had proposed fixes. Its collapse drove research into bridge aerodynamics that has shaped long-span bridge design since.

ntsc-monochrome-standard-1941.summary: In March 1941 the NTSC set America's black-and-white television standard at 525 lines, based on the Radio Manufacturers Association's 1936 recommendation; it lasted until digital switch-off in 2009. It selected 525 scan lines as its compromise between RCA's 441-line system, used by its NBC network, and Philco and DuMont's push for 605 to 800 lines, with 30 frames per second sent as two interlaced fields of 262.5 lines each. NTSC's second standard, in December 1953, added color while remaining compatible with existing black-and-white sets.

It is a polyester-family thermoplastic resin. ICI commercialized its fibre as Terylene in the 1940s; DuPont first produced Dacron fibre in 1950 and trademarked Mylar film in June 1951. Known as polyester in clothing and PET in packaging, it fills soft-drink bottles and blends with cotton in apparel; it is now the most common polyester thermoplastic, with global production of 31 million tons in 2025.

smith-putnam-wind-turbine-1941.summary: In October 1941 a 1.25-megawatt turbine on a Vermont hilltop fed wind power into a grid, the first megawatt-scale wind machine. The S. Morgan Smith Company built it as history's first megawatt-size wind turbine. Two eight-ton steel blades spanned 175 feet downwind of its 120-foot lattice tower, and its synchronous generator fed loads up to 700 kW. It ran about 1,000 hours before bearing failure in February 1943; on March 26, 1945, one blade broke at a known weak point left unreinforced by wartime shortages.

Under a microscope he saw tiny hooks catching in loops of fabric and fur. He named it velcro, from the French velours and crochet, velvet and hook. Clothing makers resisted its appearance at first; its first break came in aerospace, helping astronauts in and out of bulky space suits.

zuse-z3-1941.summary: In 1941 Konrad Zuse's Z3 ran programs on 2,600 telephone relays in Berlin, the first working programmable digital computer. Designed in 1938, it was presented on May 12, 1941, and used 2,600 relays operating at about 5–10 Hz with 22-bit floating point words, exception handling and a square root instruction; programs were stored on punched film and initial values entered by hand. Never put into everyday use, it ran a matrix program to solve aircraft wing flutter problems, and Zuse's request for funding to replace relays with electronic switches was denied.

On Mercury, engineers Powell and Donovan send robot Speedy to fetch selenium for their failing life support; a weakly worded order under Asimov's Second Law collides with a strengthened Third Law of self-preservation near a dangerous pool, so Speedy circles it until Powell exposes himself to danger and the First Law breaks that standoff. Collected in I, Robot in 1950, its Laws have shaped fiction and debate about robot ethics since.

atanasoff-berry-computer-1942.summary: In 1942 the Atanasoff-Berry Computer in Iowa solved equations electronically with binary digits; a court later called it the first computer. John Vincent Atanasoff and Clifford Berry built it in the basement of Iowa State College's physics building, where construction and testing took place from 1939 to 1942. Designed only to solve systems of up to 29 simultaneous linear equations, it was the first to do arithmetic with vacuum tubes, computed in binary and stored numbers on two rotating drums of 1,600 capacitors each, refreshed every turn, an early regenerative memory; it was not programmable, and its paper card storage for intermediate results proved unreliable.

About 30 people assembled it in November 1942; hired high school dropouts machined 45,000 graphite blocks enclosing 19,000 pieces of uranium, graphite slowing neutrons so natural uranium could sustain fission.

grand-coulee-dam-1942.summary: In 1942 Grand Coulee Dam was completed, the largest concrete structure on Earth; its power smelted the aluminium for America's warplanes. Built between 1933 and 1942, this concrete gravity dam on Washington state's Columbia River was designed to produce hydroelectric power and pump irrigation water; 1920s debate between a gravity canal and a high dam with pumps ended with dam supporters winning in 1933. Its power fed growing Pacific Northwest industries during World War II. Its reservoir, Franklin Delano Roosevelt Lake, forced over 3,000 people from their homes, including Native Americans whose lands were flooded, and it was built without fish passage.

Developed from Igor Sikorsky's experimental VS-300 as his VS-316, it received Army designation XR-4, first flew on 14 January 1942 and was accepted on 30 May 1942. A two-seat light helicopter with a single three-bladed main rotor driven by a radial engine, it was first among helicopters used by United States Army Air Forces, Navy and Coast Guard units and by Britain's Royal Air Force and Royal Navy.

us-synthetic-rubber-program-1942.summary: In 1942, cut off from Asian rubber, the United States built 51 synthetic rubber plants in two years. Rubber was needed for tires, hoses, seals and belts on military vehicles and aircraft, so America turned to synthetic elastomers made from petroleum byproducts, above all styrene-butadiene rubber. With government sponsorship, a consortium of rubber and oil companies agreed with federal representatives on March 26, 1942, on a "mutual recipe" for GR-S (Government Rubber-Styrene). Annual output of general purpose synthetic rubber rose from 231 tons in 1941 to about 920,000 tons in 1945.

us-synthetic-rubber-program-1942.detail: Styrene-butadiene rubber is formed by copolymerizing styrene and 1,3-butadiene. The recipe was 75 percent butadiene and 25 percent styrene, with potassium persulfate as initiator, soap as emulsifier, water and a dodecyl mercaptan modifier. It drew on German Buna S research, because Buna S could be mixed with natural rubber and milled on existing machines. The Baruch Rubber Survey Committee's September 1942 report called for one rubber director with full authority and for 51 plants to make its monomers and polymers; Firestone, B. F. Goodrich, Goodyear, Standard Oil of New Jersey and United States Rubber took part, and 85 percent of 1945 output was GR-S.

Before Pearl Harbor, America's Coordinator of Information office had fed war news to private shortwave stations through Robert E. Sherwood's Foreign Information Service; VOA used shortwave and shared BBC medium-wave transmitters in Britain. Control passed in mid-1942 to Office of War Information staff, in 1945 to State Department officials and in 1953 to the U.S. Information Agency.

Biro had patented the idea in Britain in 1938; an Argentine filing of 17 April 1943 became US patent 2,390,636 in 1945. The Royal Air Force ordered 30,000 because they did not leak at altitude. He described this 'Hou process' in 1943 and patented it abroad; Chinese plants adopted it after 1949 and it remains in use for soda and fertiliser in China. With America at war, TWA's order became C-69 military transports. Its triple tail, dolphin-shaped fuselage and four 18-cylinder Wright R-3350 engines became familiar after 1945, when Constellations became the first civil airliner family in widespread use with pressurized cabins, flying above most bad weather.

sigsaly-1943.summary: In 1943 SIGSALY encrypted Churchill's and Roosevelt's calls by turning speech into digits, the first digital voice link. Existing telephone scramblers were cracked by both sides, so Bell Telephone Laboratories built a prototype under A. B. Clark, assisted by British mathematician Alan Turing, and won an Army contract for two systems in 1942. It encoded speech digitally, in history's first transmission of speech by pulse-code modulation: its vocoder reduced voice to a dozen slow signals, which were masked with random noise recorded on phonograph records used as one-time pads and played on precisely synchronized turntables at both ends.

streptomycin-1943.summary: In October 1943 Albert Schatz, working in Selman Waksman's soil-screening programme at Rutgers, isolated streptomycin, the first drug to cure tuberculosis; sanatoria emptied. A PhD student in a project funded by Merck and Co., he drew it from soil bacterium Streptomyces griseus. Streptomycin binds bacterial ribosomes' 30S subunit and blocks protein synthesis, acting on both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, and it was tuberculosis's first antibiotic cure. Rutgers researchers published in January 1944, and from 1946 to 1948 Britain's Medical Research Council ran what is often cited as history's first randomized curative trial.

teleology-paper-1943.summary: In 1943 Rosenblueth, Wiener and Bigelow argued that purpose in animals and machines is feedback toward a goal. Rosenblueth was lead author. Their paper classified behavior as active or passive, active behavior as purposeful or random, and purposeful behavior as guided or not by negative feedback, so that machines steering toward targets and animals pursuing prey could be described in one language. Wiener said it set the bases for cybernetics, and he dedicated his 1948 book Cybernetics to Rosenblueth, "for many years my companion in science."

watson-five-computers-myth-1943.summary: In 1943 IBM's Thomas Watson supposedly said the world might want five computers; no record shows he said it, and the line lived on anyway. In 1943 computer usually meant a person who calculated, and biographer Kevin Maney found no speech, document or contemporary article containing those words. Its earliest known attribution appeared in Der Spiegel on May 22, 1965, describing an estimate of maximum demand of five in America's economy as commercial machines appeared in the early 1950s. Described as myth by 1973, it survives as a favorite example of failed prediction.

avery-macleod-mccarty-1944.summary: In 1944 Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that DNA, not protein, carries heredity. Frederick Griffith had shown in 1928 that some "transforming principle" could change one pneumococcal type into another, and most scientists assumed proteins carried heredity. Treatments that destroyed protein or RNA did not eliminate the extract's transforming power, while a DNA-degrading preparation did. Acceptance came slowly; Erwin Chargaff's finding that base composition varies by species and Hershey and Chase's 1952 experiment moved geneticists to accept DNA as genetic material.

borlaug-mexico-wheat-program-1944.summary: Norman Borlaug arrives in Mexico in September 1944 to lead wheat research in the Rockefeller Foundation's cooperative program with the Mexican Ministry of Agriculture, when Mexico imports half its wheat and stem rust ruins harvests. He grows two generations a year by shuttling seed between Chapingo and Sonora's Yaqui Valley, 10 degrees of latitude and 2,600 meters apart, which breaks photoperiod sensitivity and yields widely adapted lines. Rust-resistant varieties make Mexico self-sufficient in wheat by 1956. After learning in late 1952 of Orville Vogel's Norin 10 crosses, Borlaug obtains seed in 1953 and releases semi-dwarf Pitic 62 and Penjamo 62 in 1962, which carry heavy fertilizer without lodging and later seed India and Pakistan.

Mexican wheat yields rose from about 750 kilograms per hectare in 1944 to over 3,000 by the 1970s.

chicago-convention-icao-1944.summary: In December 1944 fifty-two states signed the Chicago Convention, rules of the air that let airlines fly across borders. It set rules for airspace, aircraft registration, safety and security, and Article 1 gave every state complete and exclusive sovereignty over airspace above its territory. It established the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), which came into being on April 4, 1947, after its 26th ratification on March 5, 1947; ICAO became a United Nations specialized agency that October.
