colossus-computer-1944.summary: In 1944 Colossus began breaking German cipher traffic at Bletchley Park, the first electronic digital computer, kept secret for 30 years. It became operational in January and successfully attacked its first message on 5 February 1944. General Post Office engineer Tommy Flowers designed it from plans by mathematician Max Newman to break the Lorenz cipher, which German high command used for teleprinter traffic British codebreakers called Tunny. Using thermionic valves for Boolean and counting operations against message tapes read at 1,000 to 2,000 characters per second, Colossus is regarded as history's first programmable electronic digital computer.

harvard-mark-i-1944.summary: In May 1944 Harvard's Mark I began computing for the Navy; Grace Hopper programmed it. Howard Aiken had proposed it to IBM in November 1937, drawing on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, and IBM built it at Endicott, New York: 765,000 switches, relays, shafts and clutches in a frame 51 feet (15 metres) long, doing three additions per second and one multiplication in six seconds, reading instructions from 24-channel punched paper tape. Its first programs included John von Neumann's March 1944 check on implosion for the atomic bomb.

jet-age-era-1944.summary: In 1944 jet aircraft first entered combat; by the 1950s jets carried passengers across oceans in hours. In civil aviation it reached Britain in 1952 with scheduled de Havilland Comet flights and America later that decade. De Havilland's Comet was history's first jet airliner to fly, in 1949, and its first to offer regular transatlantic service, in 1958, while Tupolev's Soviet Tu-104 was the only jet airliner operating anywhere between 1956 and 1958.

messerschmitt-me-262-1944.summary: In 1944 the Me 262 became the first jet fighter in service, reaching a trials unit in April and combat on 25 July, 100 miles an hour faster than anything Allied. Its design began in April 1939, and it first flew on jet power on 18 July 1942, but engine problems, metallurgy and interference from Göring and Hitler, who in 1943 demanded it be built as a high-speed bomber, delayed service. Among that war's most advanced combat aircraft, it proved an effective dogfighter; German pilots claimed 542 Allied aircraft, though shortages of strategic materials left it unreliable.

messerschmitt-me-262-1944.detail: Captured examples influenced North American's F-86 Sabre, Mikoyan's MiG-15 and Boeing's B-47 Stratojet.

v2-rocket-1944.summary: In September 1944 Germany began firing V-2 rockets at London, history's first long-range guided ballistic missiles; the same rockets later reached space. Designated A4 by its builders, it ended a series of prototypes developed after Germany's Army noticed Wernher von Braun's graduate research; Hitler had ordered attacks to begin as soon as possible on 29 August 1944. From September 1944 the Wehrmacht launched more than 3,000 at Allied targets, first London and later Antwerp and Liège.

atomic-age-era-1945.summary: In July 1945 Trinity exploded the first nuclear weapon in New Mexico. Robert Oppenheimer named that test Trinity; New York Times journalist William L. Laurence, who witnessed it as Manhattan Project official journalist, wrote its first accounts and popularised talk of an atomic age. Early visions promised near-limitless power: science writer David Dietz foresaw cars running for a year on a vitamin-pill-sized pellet of atomic energy. By the late 1970s, though, nuclear power faced economic difficulties and public opposition, culminating in Three Mile Island in 1979 and Chernobyl in 1986.

bush-as-we-may-think-1945.summary: In 1945 Vannevar Bush imagined the memex, a desk that stored everything a person read and linked it by association: hypertext in outline. It described a proposed personal device for storing and consulting records and linking related items through associative trails. Bush, who had directed America's wartime science effort, urged scientists turning to peacetime work to make humanity's growing store of knowledge accessible, since inventions had so far extended physical powers more than powers of mind. It anticipated hypertext, personal computers and online encyclopedias; Douglas Engelbart read it soon after publication and kept its memex in mind in work leading to the mouse and hyperlinks.

Bush, who headed America's Office of Scientific Research and Development, which produced radar and proximity fuzes, answered that scientific progress was essential to national security, health, jobs and living standards, and proposed a National Research Foundation to fund university research. His centralized model shaped modern American science policy.

Herman Potočnik had described such orbits in 1928, but Clarke expanded on them: a satellite in circular orbit 35,786 km above Earth's equator circles once per sidereal day, so it appears fixed in the sky and ground antennas never have to track it.

Distribution bred bitter acrimony: courts later ruled it a public disclosure that made EDVAC's patent unenforceable, and Moore School engineers argued that stored-program ideas predated von Neumann's consulting.

ethiopian-airlines-founded-1945.summary: In December 1945 Ethiopia founded an airline managed by TWA; it became Africa's largest and most profitable carrier. Ethiopia's government provided its initial investment, and TWA managed it. Its first revenue scheduled service began on 8 April 1946, flying the Addis Ababa-Asmara-Cairo route. After Ethiopia's liberation, Emperor Haile Selassie I had asked the United States, Britain and France to help establish an airline as part of his modernisation effort. International flights began in 1951, Ethiopian staff took over management in 1971, and the carrier joined Star Alliance in December 2011.

fao-founded-1945.summary: In October 1945 44 governments founded the Food and Agriculture Organization to lead international efforts against hunger and improve nutrition and food security. Its first conference, led by Sir John Boyd Orr, ran to 1 November 1945. It succeeded the International Institute of Agriculture, created in Rome in 1905, urged by Polish-born American agriculturalist David Lubin, and dissolved in 1948, when its functions passed to FAO.

fao-founded-1945.detail: Headquarters moved from Washington to Rome in 1951. FAO now has 194 members, 193 countries plus the European Union, and operates in over 130 countries.

hiroshima-nagasaki-1945.summary: In August 1945 American atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing over 100,000. At about 8:15 a.m. the B-29 bomber Enola Gay released “Little Boy” over Hiroshima, where about 350,000 people were present that morning; President Truman then threatened further bombings unless Japan surrendered under his July 26 Potsdam Declaration, and “Fat Man” followed over Nagasaki. Japan accepted Potsdam's terms on August 15 and formally surrendered on September 2, 1945. These remain history's only uses of nuclear weapons in war.

operation-paperclip-1945.summary: From 1945 America brought 1,500 German scientists over, Wernher von Braun among them, under Joint Intelligence Objectives Agency oversight; their rockets took Americans to the Moon. As Allied armies advanced into Germany in 1945 they found research behind V-2 rockets, jet aircraft and other wartime advances; SHAEF's T-Force, set up in February 1945, examined 5,000 German targets. Washington wanted that expertise kept from neutral countries and, as Cold War tensions emerged, from the Soviet Union, and several recruits were confirmed former Nazi Party, SS or SA members.

trinity-nuclear-test-1945.summary: On 16 July 1945 America exploded the first atomic bomb in New Mexico, with explosive force of 25,000 tonnes of TNT. It detonated a plutonium implosion-design device yielding 25 kilotons of TNT. Its “gadget” shared its design with Fat Man, dropped on Nagasaki: following John von Neumann's September 1943 proposal, layers of faster and slower high explosives sent a single compressive wave into its plutonium core. President Truman wanted results before the Potsdam conference opened on July 16, so testing went ahead on that earliest date.

atomic-energy-act-1946.summary: In 1946 America put the atom under civilian control in a new Atomic Energy Commission; the bomb's makers answered to civilians, though a Military Liaison Committee kept considerable military influence. When it took effect on January 1, 1947, this Commission took over from the Manhattan Project. Its control-of-information section made all data on weapon design “restricted data,” classified from birth. By cutting off nuclear information to other countries it opened a rift with Britain and Canada, Manhattan Project partners, and pushed Britain to build its own weapons.

bikini-atoll-operation-crossroads-1946.summary: In February 1946 US Navy Commodore Ben Wyatt asked 167 Bikinians to leave their atoll 'for the good of mankind'; they were moved to Rongerik, where they nearly starved, and later to Kili. On 1 July 1946 Test Able dropped a 23-kiloton bomb over 95 target ships in Bikini lagoon, and on 25 July Test Baker exploded underwater, drenching fleet in radioactive spray that could not be decontaminated. Shurcliff's official 1947 report recorded results; Weisgall's history documents how Baker's contamination surprised planners. Bikini hosted 23 nuclear tests through 1958, including Castle Bravo. Niedenthal's 1997 account traces islanders' displacement, brief return in 1970s, re-evacuation in 1978 and continued exile.

eniac-1946.summary: In 1946 ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, appeared, a thousand times faster than any rival. John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert had designed the Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer to calculate artillery firing tables for the Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory, under a contract signed on 5 June 1943, though its first program studied a thermonuclear weapon's feasibility. It weighed more than 30 tons, consumed 150 kW and cost $487,000.

macy-conferences-1946.summary: From 1946 the Macy conferences brought mathematicians, biologists and engineers together to study feedback and control: cybernetics. Warren McCulloch chaired them, with responsibility for seeing that disciplinary boundaries were crossed, and they brought together researchers to discuss feedback, circular causality, and biological and social systems. The first met on 8–9 March 1946; participants discussed research still in progress rather than finished papers, and widely circulated transcripts spread their conversation. Aiming at a general science of how human minds work, these meetings spawned breakthroughs in systems theory, cybernetics and what became cognitive science.

mobile-telephone-service-1946.summary: In June 1946 the first car telephone service opened in St Louis; a handful of calls at a time could be made from the road. Bell System's service needed operators in both directions: landline callers reached a mobile operator who announced each call over its shared channel, and mobile users asked that operator to place outgoing calls. Improved Mobile Telephone Service replaced it from 1964, though MTS stayed in use in places into the 1980s.

tupperware-1946.summary: In 1946 Earl Tupper moulded his first airtight polyethylene container; sold at home parties from 1948, it put plastic in every kitchen. His airtight, food-safe plastic containers were aimed at consumers. From 1951, with former Stanley Home Products saleswoman Brownie Wise as vice president of Tupperware Home Parties, Tupperware sold mainly through home “Tupperware parties”, promoted since 1948, which let women of the 1950s earn income without holding a regular job; parties reached Europe in 1960. Parent company Tupperware Brands filed for bankruptcy in September 2024, and Party Products LLC, formed by its lenders, bought the brand that November.

volta-redonda-csn-1946.summary: In 1946 Brazil's state steelworks at Volta Redonda, in Rio de Janeiro state, began production with American wartime loans under President Eurico Gaspar Dutra, initially making coke, pig iron castings and long products. Brazil and America had agreed, in the Washington Accords, that its Presidente Vargas Steelworks would supply steel to Allied forces in World War II and support Brazil's development afterward. Brazil's government privatized it in 1993 and early 1994, and CSN is now Brazil's largest fully integrated steel producer.

automation-term-ford-1947.summary: In April 1947 Ford set up an Automation Department, and the word entered English; within ten years it named a national anxiety. Harder is credited with coining “automation.” Five staff grew to fifty within a year, working first on engines and later on sheet metal, wheels, axles and frames; relay controls modernized transfer lines that moved engine blocks between machining stages. Usage spread widely after John Diebold's 1952 book Automation: The Advent of the Automatic Factory; American audiences were fixated on this new word for nearly two decades after 1947.

bell-x1-sound-barrier-1947.summary: In October 1947 Chuck Yeager flew Bell's X-1 faster than sound; the barrier was a myth and supersonic flight followed. His aircraft, nicknamed Glamorous Glennis for his wife, was rocket-powered and shaped like a .50-caliber machine gun bullet, known to be stable at supersonic speed; it was drop launched from a B-29 bomber's bomb bay and glided down to a dry lake bed once its engine burned out. News stayed secret until Aviation Week and the Los Angeles Times reported it in December 1947.

cellular-concept-1947.summary: In 1947 a Bell Labs memo proposed splitting a city into cells with their own transmitters so frequencies could be reused: mobile networks. In such a network, service territory is divided into cells, each served by its own base station, and a switching system developed by Amos Joel at Bell Labs lets many callers share one frequency by handing calls to the nearest tower with that frequency free, so scarce radio spectrum is reused across cells. Japan's NTT launched history's first commercial cellular network in Tokyo in 1979; regulatory battles delayed AT&T's commercial service until 1983.

celorio-tortilla-machine-1947.summary: In 1947 Mexican inventor Fausto Celorio receives Mexican patent 45,792 for a machine that presses masa into discs and carries them on a conveyor belt through a gas-fired cooking tunnel, as a later US patent in this lineage describes. Earlier machines from 1904 had cut and cooked tortillas but jammed on dough; Celorio's rollers and continuous belt made production reliable. He built about one machine a month in the early 1950s, then forty a week in partnership with Alfonso Gandara, and in 1963 introduced a duplex model producing 132 kg an hour. Corner tortillerias with clattering belts became part of Mexican urban life, and machines like his are exported across the Americas.

doomsday-clock-1947.summary: In 1947 atomic scientists set the Doomsday Clock at seven minutes to midnight, a gauge of how close humanity stood to destruction. Manhattan Project scientists in Chicago had founded that magazine in 1945, and Langsdorf, whose husband Alexander Langsdorf Jr. had worked on that project, chose a clock to convey urgency: midnight stands for human-made global catastrophe, and she set its hands at seven minutes to midnight. Its publishers have reset it 27 times since, as far back as 17 minutes in 1991 and, in 2026, to 85 seconds, its closest setting yet.
